nodes.statement: (Forwards.) Trivial. (Backwards.) By contraposition, suppose e is a non-trivial endomorphism of a reflexive tournament ensuremathH. Consider e(ensuremathH) and build some function e^-1 from e(ensuremathH) to ensuremathH by choosing e^-1(y)=x if e(x)=y arbitrarily. Since ensuremathH is a (reflexive) tournament, e^-1 is an isomorphism, whereupon e^-1 circ e is the identity automorphism when restricted to some subtournament ensuremathH_0 of ensuremathH. nodes.statement: (1) As any reflexive digraph can be retracted onto a double edge, the result follows. \\[3pt] (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume ensuremathH is weakly connected. If~ensuremathH is not strongly connected, then ensuremathH has an edge (a,b) such that a and b are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from b to a. We define a retraction of ensuremathH onto the subgraph induced by \a,b\ as follows: let r(x) = a if there exists a directed path from x to a and r(x)=b otherwise. As r(a)=a and r(b)=b, it remains to check if r is an endomorphism. Let (x,y) be an edge. If r(y)=a, then there exists a directed path from y to~a, and thus a directed path from x to~a implying that r(a)=a. If r(y)=b, then r(x)=a and r(x)=b are both allowed.\\[3pt] (3) We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism sigma backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that (sigma,c) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH) for some constant map c, say for all uin V(ensuremathH), c(u)=v for some vin V(ensuremathH). By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~, we obtain that (id_ensuremathH,c) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH). Since ensuremathH is strongly connected, every vertex uin V(ensuremathH) has out-degree at least~1. Hence (u,v) in E(ensuremathH) for all u in V(ensuremathH). Since v has out-degree at least~1, this means that ensuremathH contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1). Now suppose that there exists an automorphism sigma that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism f neq sigma (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have (sigma,f) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH). Apply sigma^-1 to both sides of the edge to obtain that (id_ensuremathH,g) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH) for some g neq id_ensuremathH. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that ensuremathH is retract-trivial, this means g is a constant map, contradicting the claim above.

nodes.statement: Since ensuremathH is endo-trivial, ensuremathH is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~, ensuremathH is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of ensuremathH are isolated vertices of~widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. As ensuremathH is endo-trivial, this means that widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH is the disjoint union of a copy of ensuremathH that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of ensuremathH. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an n-ary polymorphism~f of ensuremathH which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~f depends on all of its n variables, where n geq 2. By Lemma~, the mapping F:ensuremathH^n-1 rightarrow widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH defined by F(x_1,ldots,x_n-1)(y) = f(x_1,ldots,x_n-1,y) is a homomorphism. Since ensuremathH is strongly connected, so is ensuremathH^n-1, and hence so is the image of F in widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case f does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case f does not depend on any of its first n-1 variables.

First, take a copy of ensuremathH together with ensuremathG and build ensuremathG' by identifying these on the copy of ensuremathH_0 that they both possess as a subgraph. Let m be the size of ensuremathH_0 and consider its Hamilton cycle HC_0. We build ensuremathG'' from ensuremathG' by augmenting a new copy of Cylm for every vertex v in V(ensuremathG') setminus V(ensuremathH_0). Vertex~v is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of DCm in Cylm and the bottom copy of DCm is to be identified with HC_0 in ensuremathH_0 according to the identity function. First suppose that ensuremathG retracts to ensuremathH_0. Let h be a retraction from ensuremathG to ensuremathH_0. We extend h as follows. First we map the copy of ensuremathH in ensuremathG'' to itself in ensuremathH by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of Cylm in ensuremathG''. This is always possible: because ensuremathH retracts to ensuremathH_0, we have Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0])=V(ensuremathH) due to Lemma~. This leads to a surjective homomorphism from ensuremathG'' to ensuremathH. Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~h from ensuremathG'' to ensuremathH. Now, 1<|h(ensuremathH_0)|<m is not possible either due to Lemma~. Thus, |h(ensuremathH_0)|=m and indeed h maps ensuremathH_0 to a copy of itself in ensuremathH which we will call ensuremathH'_0=i(ensuremathH_0) for some isomorphism~i. As h is surjective, there exists a vertex~xin V(ensuremathG'') with h(x)=y. By construction, x belongs to some copy of DCm, and thus also belongs to some copy of DCm in ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0). Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ be an instance of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$-{\sc Retraction}.
We build an instance~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ of {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}
in the following fashion. First, take a copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ together with $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by identifying these on the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ that they both possess as a subgraph.
Let $m$ be the size of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ and consider its Hamilton cycle $\HC_0$. We build $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$ by augmenting a new copy of $\Cylm$ for every vertex
$v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}') \setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$. 
Vertex~$v$ is to be identified with any vertex in the top copy of $\DCm$ in $\Cylm$ and the bottom copy of $\DCm$ is to be identified with $\HC_0$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ according to the identity function.
See Figure~\ref{f-new} for an example.
We claim that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ if and only if there exists a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$  to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

First suppose that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.
Let $h$ be a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. We extend $h$ as follows. First we map the copy of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by the identity. This will ensure surjectivity. We then map the various copies of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This is always possible: because $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ retracts to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$, we have $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0])=V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ due to Lemma~\ref{lem:spillage}. Hence, if $h(x)=y$ for two vertices $x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ and $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we can always find a retraction of the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that maps $x$ to $y$, and we mimic this retraction on the corresponding subgraph in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. The crucial observation is that this can be done independently for each vertex in $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}')\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, as two vertices of different copies of $\Cylm$ are only adjacent if they both belong to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'$.
This leads to a surjective homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.

Now suppose that there exists a surjective homomorphism~$h$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$  to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$.
If $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=1$, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:claim1}, $|h(\Cylm)|=1$ for all copies of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}''$. This means that $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')|=1$ and $h$ is not surjective, a contradiction. Now, $1<|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|<m$ is not possible either due to Lemma~\ref{lem:under-m}. Thus, $|h(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)|=m$ and indeed $h$ maps $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ to a copy of itself in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ which we will call $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0=i(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$ for some isomorphism~$i$. 

We claim that $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. In order to see this, consider a vertex $y\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. 
As $h$ is surjective, there exists a vertex~$x\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}'')$ with $h(x)=y$. By construction, $x$ belongs to some copy of $\DCm$, and thus also belongs to some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$.
We can extend $i^{-1}$ to an isomorphism from the copy of $\Cylm$  (which has $i(\HC_0)$ as its bottom cycle)  in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to the copy of $\Cylm$ (which has $\HC_0$ as its bottom cycle) in the graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$.
We define a mapping~$r^*$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ by $r^*(u)=h\circ i^{-1}(u)$ if $u$ is on the copy of $\Cylm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ and $r^*(u)=u$ otherwise. We observe that $r^*(u)=u$ if $u\in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0')$ as $h$ coincides with $i$ on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$. As $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ separates the other vertices of 
the copy of $\Cylm$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})\setminus V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0)$, in the sense that removing $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$ would disconnect them, this means that $r^*$ is a retraction from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0',i(\HC_0))$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. We find that $r^*$ maps $i(x)$ to $h\circ i^{-1}(i(x))=h(x)=y$. Moreover, as $x$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0,\HC_0)$, we have that $i(x)$ is in some copy of $\DCm$ in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0))$. We may assume without loss of generality that $i(x)$ belongs to the top copy (cf. Remark~1). We conclude that $y$ always belongs to  $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)])$ (cf. Remark~1).

As $\mathrm{Spill}_m(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}[\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0,i(\HC_0)]) = V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, we find, by assumption of the lemma, that there exists a retraction $r$ from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'_0$.  
Now $i^{-1} \circ r \circ h$ ia the desired retraction of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}_0$.

Recall the self-map digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}}$, with vertices the self-maps of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$, and an edge $(f,g) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ between self-maps $f$ and $g$ if and only if for every edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, we have that $(f(x),g(y)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
In the self-map digraph, the endomorphisms are precisely the looped vertices.

Consider the homomorphism $\varphi: \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ induced by an $n+1$-ary polymorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ where $n \geq 1$; suppose for a contradiction that the polymorphism depends on all its variables. Then clearly the image of $\varphi$ contains at least two elements, and at least one of these elements is not a constant map.  

\noindent{\bf Claim 0.} {\em The only loops in $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ are the constant maps 1 and 2 and the identity. }

\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 0}: let $f$ be an endomorphism of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. Then $f$ maps loops to loops. Since $(1,2)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, $f$ can either map both to 1, both to 2 , or fix both. Clearly if it fixes both $f$ is the identity. Otherwise, if $f(1)=f(2)=i$, then $(f(0),i) , (i,f(0)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=i$. 

Without fear of confusion, we denote the constant maps by 0, 1 and 2. We denote the identity map by $id$.

\noindent{\bf Claim 1.} {\em (a) There are no edges in  $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^{\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}}$ between the identity and the constant maps; (b) if $(2,f), (f,1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, then $f=0$; (c) if $c$ is a constant map such that $(f,c),(c,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = c$. }



\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 1}:  $(2,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(i)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ for all $i$ so $f(i) \in \{0,2\}$ for all $i$. Similarly $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ so (b) follows immediately. To prove (a), observe that any in- or out-neighbour of a constant cannot be surjective since no constant has in- or out-neighbourhood of size 3. For (c), argue again as we just did: $(1,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ means $f(i) \in \{1,2\}$ for all $i$, and $(f,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $f(i) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $i$ and hence $f=1$; the proof for $c=2$ is identical.  



\noindent{\bf Claim 2.} {\em If $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ then $f = id$. }

\noindent {\em Proof of Claim 2}: Assume that $(f,id),(id,f) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. If $i$ is a loop then $(i,i)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(i),i),(i,f(i))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$  thus $f(i) = i$. Now $(0,1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(f(0),1)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$, and $(2,0)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ implies $(2,f(0))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so $f(0)=0$. 


Obviously the loops of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ are precisely the tuples whose coordinates belong to $\{1,2\}$. Call the subdigraph induced by these vertices $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$, and notice it is weakly connected. Then the homomorphism $\varphi$ must map $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$  onto a weakly connected digraph consisting of loops only. By Claim 1 (a) either  (i) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is entirely mapped to $\{id\}$ or (ii) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is mapped by $\varphi$ to the set $\{1,2\}$.

Choose any tuple $X$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ containing a coordinate equal to 0. Then there exist $Y, Z \in W$ such that $(X,Z), (Z,Y), (Y,X) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n)$: indeed, let $Z$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each  0 entry by 1, fixing all other coordinates, and let $Y$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each 0 entry by 2, fixing all other coordinates. Thus in case (i) we get that $id = \varphi(Y), (\varphi(Y),\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),\varphi(Z)) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ and $\varphi(Z)=id$ so by Claim 2 $\varphi$ maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to $id$. In case (ii), we get that $\varphi(Y)$ and $\varphi(Z)$ belong to $\{1,2\}$; since $(\varphi(Z),\varphi(Y))\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ we must in fact have that $(\varphi(Z),\varphi(Y))$ belongs to $\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2)\}$; thus we get one of the following cases, namely $(1,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),1) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ or $(1,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),2) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ or $(2,\varphi(X)),(\varphi(X),2) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$. By Claim 1 (b) and (c)  $\varphi(X)$ must be one of the constant maps 0, 1 or 2. 

Thus we conclude that $\varphi$ either maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to $\{id\}$, in which case our polymorphism cannot depend on its first $n$ variables; or otherwise $\varphi$ maps all of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n$ to constant maps, and then the polymorphism does not depend on its last variable, also a contradiction.

As discussed, we only need to settle the complexity of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} for the digraphs depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs}, as for all other partially reflexive digraphs of size at most $3$, {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in P \cite{FederHellTucker}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (a), (c) or (d), then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an irreflexive semicomplete digraph with more than one cycle and it is known from \cite{Semicomplete} that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \NP-hard, thus the same can be said for both {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the partially reflexive tree of Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (b), {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is known to be \NP-hard from \cite{pseudoforests} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is known to be \NP-hard from \cite{GolovachPS12}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the reflexive tournament from Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (e), the result follows from Corollary~\ref{c-main} or Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. For the related case (f), we appeal to Lemma~\ref{lem:case-f} (finishing via Corollary~\ref{c-main}).

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (g), membership in \Ptime\ for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, and therefore {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:case-g}, in light of the recent groundbreaking proofs of \cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}.

Then the homomorphism $\varphi$ must map $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$  onto a weakly connected digraph consisting of loops only. By Claim 1 (a) either  (i) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is entirely mapped to $\{id\}$ or (ii) $\ensuremath{\mathrm{W}}$ is mapped by $\varphi$ to the set $\{1,2\}$.

Then there exist $Y, Z \in W$ such that $(X,Z), (Z,Y), (Y,X) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}^n)$: indeed, let $Z$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each  0 entry by 1, fixing all other coordinates, and let $Y$ be obtained from $X$ by replacing each 0 entry by 2, fixing all other coordinates. As discussed, we only need to settle the complexity of {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} for the digraphs depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs}, as for all other partially reflexive digraphs of size at most $3$, {\sc List $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is in P \cite{FederHellTucker}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (a), (c) or (d), then $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is an irreflexive semicomplete digraph with more than one cycle and it is known from \cite{Semicomplete} that {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \NP-hard, thus the same can be said for both {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the partially reflexive tree of Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (b), {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} is known to be \NP-hard from \cite{pseudoforests} and {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is known to be \NP-hard from \cite{GolovachPS12}.

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is the reflexive tournament from Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (e), the result follows from Corollary~\ref{c-main} or Lemma~\ref{prop:main1}. For the related case (f), we appeal to Lemma~\ref{lem:case-f} (finishing via Corollary~\ref{c-main}).

When $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:3digraphs} (g), membership in \Ptime\ for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction}, and therefore {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring}, follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:case-g}, in light of the recent groundbreaking proofs of \cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement: This paper concerns the computational complexity of the surjective homomorphism problem, also known in the literature as sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring and sc ensuremathH-Vertex-Compaction . This problem requires the homomorphism to be surjective. It is a cousin of the list homomorphism problem and is even more closely related to the retraction and compaction problems. Indeed, the sc ensuremathH-Compaction problem, hitherto defined only for graphs~ensuremathH, takes as input a graph ensuremathG and asks if there exists a function f from V(ensuremathG) to V(ensuremathH) so that for each non-loop edge (x,y) in E(ensuremathH) (mboxi.e. with xneq y), there exists u,v in V(ensuremathG) so that f(u)=x and f(v)=y. Thus, compaction can be seen as the edge-surjective homomorphism problem.footnoteExcept for the treatment of self-loops, which appears to be an idiosyncrasy that plays no vital role in computational complexity. For some history of the definition see . The problem sc ensuremathH-Retraction takes as input a superstructure~ensuremathG of ensuremathH and asks whether there is a homomorphism from ensuremathG to ensuremathH that is the identity on ensuremathH. The sc ensuremathH-Retraction problem is polynomially equivalent with a special type of CSP, CSP(ensuremathH'), where ensuremathH' is ensuremathH decorated with constants naming the elements of its domain. Feder and Vardi showed that the task of classifying the complexities of the retraction problems is equivalent to that for the CSPs. Hence, owing to , sc ensuremathH-Retraction has now been fully classified.

This paper concerns the computational complexity of 
the \emph{surjective homomorphism} problem, also known in the literature as {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} \cite{CiE2017,GolovachPS12} and {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Vertex-Compaction} \cite{VikasAlgorithmica}. This problem requires the homomorphism
to be surjective.
It is a cousin of the \emph{list homomorphism} problem and is even more closely related to the \emph{retraction} and \emph{compaction} problems. Indeed, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Compaction} problem, hitherto defined only for graphs~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, takes as input a graph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ and asks if there exists a function $f$ from $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ to $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ so that for each non-loop edge $(x,y) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}})$ (\mbox{i.e.} with $x\neq y$), there exists $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ so that $f(u)=x$ and $f(v)=y$. Thus, compaction can be seen as the \emph{edge-surjective homomorphism} problem.\footnote{Except for the treatment of self-loops, which appears to be an idiosyncrasy that plays no vital role in computational complexity. For some history of the definition see \cite{VikasReflexive}.} The problem {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} takes as input a superstructure~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ and asks whether there is a homomorphism from $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ to $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ that is the identity on $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$. 
The {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is polynomially equivalent with a special type of CSP, CSP$(\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}')$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}'$ is $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ decorated with constants naming the elements of its domain.
 Feder and Vardi~\cite{FederVardi} showed that
the task of classifying the complexities of the retraction problems is equivalent to that for the CSPs. 
Hence, owing to ~\cite{FVproofBulatov,FVproofZhuk}, {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} has now been fully classified.

nodes.statement: Reflexive tournaments form an important subclass of the class of reflexive semicomplete graphs and are well-understood algebraically. In particular, the classification for sc ensuremathH-Retraction where ensuremathH is a reflexive tournament can be inferred from the algebraic characterisation from: for a reflexive tournament~ensuremathH, the sc ensuremathH-Retraction problem is in NL if ensuremathH is transitive, and it is NP-complete otherwise. This raises the question whether the same holds for sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring and whether we can develop algebraic methods further to prove this. In fact, the algebraic method is by now well known for CSPs and their relatives, including its use with digraphs; see the recent survey . However, the algebraic method is not so far advanced for surjective homomorphism problems. So far it only exists in the work of Chen, who proved that sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring is NP-complete if ensuremathH has the property that all of its polymorphisms depend only on one variable, that is, are essentially unary. Chen's result has not yet been put to work (even on toy open problems) and a key driver for our research has been to find, in the wild, a place for its application.

Reflexive tournaments form an important subclass of the class of reflexive semicomplete graphs
and are well-understood algebraically~\cite{larose2006taylor}.  
In particular,
the classification for {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is a reflexive tournament can be inferred from 
the algebraic characterisation from~\cite{larose2006taylor}: for a reflexive tournament~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$, the {\sc $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Retraction} problem is in NL if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ is transitive, and it is \NP-complete otherwise. This raises the question whether the same holds for {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} and whether we can develop algebraic methods further to prove this.
In fact, the algebraic method is by now well known for CSPs and their relatives, including its use with digraphs; see the recent survey \cite{LaroseSurvey17}. However, the algebraic method is not so far advanced for surjective homomorphism problems.
So far it only exists in the work of Chen~\cite{ChenSurHom}, who proved that {\sc Surjective $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$-Colouring} is \NP-complete if $\ensuremath{\mathrm{H}}$ 
has the property that all of its polymorphisms depend only on one variable, that is, are essentially unary. 
Chen's result has not yet been put to work (even on toy open problems) and a key driver for our research has been to find, in the wild, a place for its application.

nodes.statement: The directed path on k vertices is the digraph with vertices u_0,ldots, u_k-1 and edges (u_i,u_i+1) for i=0,ldots,k-2. The directed cycle on k vertices is obtained from the directed path on k vertices after adding the edge (u_k-1,u_0). A digraph ensuremathG is strongly connected if for all u,v in V(ensuremathG) there is a directed path in E(ensuremathG) from u to v (note that we take this to include the situation u=v, but for reflexive graphs the distinction is moot). A digraph is weakly connected if its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected. A double-edge in a digraph ensuremathG consists in a pair of distinct vertices u,v in V(ensuremathG), so that (u,v),(v,u) in E(ensuremathG). A digraph ensuremathG is semicomplete if for every two distinct vertices u and v, at least one of (u,v), (v,u) belongs to E(ensuremathG). A digraph~ensuremathG is a tournament if for every two distinct vertices u and v, exactly one of (u,v), (v,u) belongs to E(ensuremathG). We demand our tournaments have more than one vertex (to rule out certain trivial cases in proofs). A reflexive tournament ensuremathG is transitive if for every triple of vertices u,v,w with (u,v), (v,w)in E(ensuremathG), also (u,w) belongs to E(ensuremathG). A digraph~ensuremathF is a subgraph of a digraph ensuremathG if V(ensuremathF) subseteq V(ensuremathG) and E(ensuremathF) subseteq E(ensuremathG). It is induced if E(ensuremathF) coincides with E(ensuremathG) restricted to pairs containing only vertices of V(ensuremathF). A subtournament is an induced subgraph of a tournament (note that this is a fortiori a tournament). All subgraphs we consider in this paper will be induced.

The \emph{directed path} on $k$ vertices is the digraph with vertices $u_0,\ldots, u_{k-1}$ and edges $(u_i,u_{i+1})$ for $i=0,\ldots,k-2$.
The \emph{directed cycle} on $k$ vertices is obtained from the directed path on $k$ vertices after adding the edge $(u_{k-1},u_0)$.
A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{strongly connected} if for all $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ there is a 
directed path 
in $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ from $u$ to $v$ (note that we take this to include the situation $u=v$, but for reflexive graphs the distinction is moot). A digraph is \emph{weakly connected} if its symmetric closure (underlying undirected graph) is connected. A \emph{double-edge} in a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ consists in a pair of distinct vertices $u,v \in V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, so that $(u,v),(v,u) \in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
A digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{semicomplete} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, at least one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. 
A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is a \emph{tournament} if for every two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, exactly one of $(u,v)$, $(v,u)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
We demand our tournaments have more than one vertex (to rule out certain trivial cases in proofs). A reflexive tournament $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ is \emph{transitive} if for every triple of vertices $u,v,w$ with $(u,v), (v,w)\in E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$, also $(u,w)$ belongs to $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$.
 A digraph~$\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}$ is a \emph{subgraph} of a digraph $\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}}$ if $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ and $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}}) \subseteq E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$. It is \emph{induced} if $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$ coincides with $E(\ensuremath{\mathrm{G}})$ restricted to pairs containing only vertices of $V(\ensuremath{\mathrm{F}})$. A \emph{subtournament} is an induced subgraph of a tournament (note that this is a fortiori a tournament). All subgraphs we consider in this paper will be induced.

nodes.statement: Let ensuremathG be a digraph. An endomorphism of~ensuremathG is a homomorphism from ensuremathG to itself. An endomorphism~e of ensuremathG is a constant map if there exists a vertex vin V(ensuremathG) such that e(u)=v for all uin V(ensuremathG). The endomorphism digraph widehatensuremathG^ensuremathG is the restriction of the self-map digraph ensuremathG^ensuremathG to the vertices induced by endomorphisms of ensuremathG. Note that the self-loops of ensuremathG^ensuremathG are precisely the endomorphisms of ensuremathG, so widehatensuremathG^ensuremathG is reflexive when ensuremathG is reflexive. We now make two more observations. The first one follows directly from the definition of widehatensuremathG^ensuremathG as well. The second one can, for example, be found in Section~5.2 of.

nodes.statement: We note that every endo-trivial structure is also retract-trivial. However, the reverse implication is not necessarily true: in Figure~ we give an example of a structure that is retract-trivial but not endo-trivial. nodes.statement: Let 3NRC be the hypergraph with vertex-set \r,g,b\ and hyperedge-set \r,g,b\setminus\(r,g,b),(r,b,g),(g,b,r),(g,r,b),(b,r,g),(b,g,r)\. Then sc 3-No-Rainbow-Colouring is the problem sc Surjective 3NRC-Colouring, in which one looks for a surjective colouring of the vertices, such that no hyperedge is rainbow-coloured (mboxi.e. uses all colours). We recall that the complexity of this problem is open since it arose (under a different name) in , see also Question~3 in. The sc Surjective DC^*_3-Colouring problem is the digraph problem most closely related to sc 3-No-Rainbow-Colouring. To explain this, when looking for digraphs with a similar character to 3NRC, we would insist at least that the automorphism group is transitive. This leaves just the reflexive and irreflexive directed 3-cycles and the reflexive and irreflexive 3-cliques, that is, 3-cycles with a double edge between every pair of vertices (admittedly, the cycles have only some of the automorphisms of the cliques). If~ensuremathH is the reflexive 3-clique, then ensuremathH-sc Retraction and sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring are trivial. If~ensuremathH is the irreflexive directed 3-cycle, then ensuremathH has a majority polymorphism, which shows that ensuremathH-sc Retraction, and thus sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring (see Figure~), can be solved in polynomial time. If~ensuremathH is the irreflexive 3-clique, then sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring is NP-complete, as there exists a straightforward reduction from 3-sc Colouring. Hence~ensuremathH=DC^*_3 was indeed the only case for which determining the complexity of sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring was not immediately obvious.

nodes.statement: 3pt] (2) A reflexive digraph that is not weakly connected may be retracted onto a 2-vertex digraph. So we may safely assume ensuremathH is weakly connected. If~ensuremathH is not strongly connected, then ensuremathH has an edge (a,b) such that a and b are in different strong components, that is, there is no directed path from b to a. We define a retraction of ensuremathH onto the subgraph induced by \a,b\ as follows: let r(x) = a if there exists a directed path from x to a and r(x)=b otherwise. As r(a)=a and r(b)=b, it remains to check if r is an endomorphism. Let (x,y) be an edge. If r(y)=a, then there exists a directed path from y to~a, and thus a directed path from x to~a implying that r(a)=a. If r(y)=b, then r(x)=a and r(x)=b are both allowed.\\[3pt] (3) We first prove that no constant map is adjacent to an automorphism in widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an automorphism sigma backwards-adjacent to some constant (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus without loss of generality we may assume that (sigma,c) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH) for some constant map c, say for all uin V(ensuremathH), c(u)=v for some vin V(ensuremathH). By composing sufficiently many times via Lemma~, we obtain that (id_ensuremathH,c) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH). Since ensuremathH is strongly connected, every vertex uin V(ensuremathH) has out-degree at least~1. Hence (u,v) in E(ensuremathH) for all u in V(ensuremathH). Since v has out-degree at least~1, this means that ensuremathH contains a double edge, contradicting statement~(1). Now suppose that there exists an automorphism sigma that is backward-adjacent to some endomorphism f neq sigma (the case of forwards-adjacent is dual). Thus, without loss of generality we have (sigma,f) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH). Apply sigma^-1 to both sides of the edge to obtain that (id_ensuremathH,g) in E(widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH) for some g neq id_ensuremathH. By the preceding lemma, and the fact that ensuremathH is retract-trivial, this means g is a constant map, contradicting the claim above. We use Lemma~ to obtain the following structural result. Let ensuremathH be an endo-trivial reflexive digraph with at least three vertices. Then every polymorphism of ensuremathH is essentially unary. Since ensuremathH is endo-trivial, ensuremathH is retract-trivial. Hence, by Lemma~, ensuremathH is strongly connected, and furthermore the automorphisms of ensuremathH are isolated vertices of~widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. As ensuremathH is endo-trivial, this means that widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH is the disjoint union of a copy of ensuremathH that corresponds to the constant maps and a set of isolated vertices, one for each automorphism of ensuremathH. Suppose for a contradiction that there exists an an n-ary polymorphism~f of ensuremathH which is not essentially unary. We may without loss of generality assume that~f depends on all of its n variables, where n geq 2. By Lemma~, the mapping F:ensuremathH^n-1 rightarrow widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH defined by F(x_1,ldots,x_n-1)(y) = f(x_1,ldots,x_n-1,y) is a homomorphism. Since ensuremathH is strongly connected, so is ensuremathH^n-1, and hence so is the image of F in widehatensuremathH^ensuremathH. Thus this image is either contained in the component of constants, in which case f does not depend on its last variable, else it is a singleton, in which case f does not depend on any of its first n-1 variables. Combining Theorems~ and~ yields the main result of this section. If ensuremathH is an endo-trivial reflexive digraph on at least three vertices, then sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring is NP-complete. Let DC^*_k denote the reflexive directed cycle on k vertices, which is readily seen to be endo-trivial. Corollary~ yields the following dichotomy for reflexive directed cycles after noting that sc Surjective DC^*_k-Colouring is trivial for kleq 2. sc Surjective DC^*_k-Colouring is in LL\ if kleq 2 and NP-complete if kgeq 3. It is not difficult to construct endo-trivial reflexive tournaments other than reflexive directed cycles. In the next section though we give a combinatorial NP-hardness proof for sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring whenever ensuremathH is any non-transitive reflexive tournament. As DC^*_3 is such a digraph, this proof also can be used for the case ensuremathH=DC^*_3. However, it does not extend to sc Surjective DC^*_k-Colouring for kgeq 4. sectionA Dichotomy for Reflexive Tournaments In this section we prove our main result, namely a dichotomy of sc Surjective ensuremathH-Colouring for reflexive tournaments~ensuremathH by showing that transitivity is the crucial property for tractability. We usually visualise the right-hand copy of DC^*_4 as the ``bottom'' copy and then we talk about vertices ``above'' and ``below'' according to the red arrows. subsectionThe NP-Hardness Gadget We now introduce the gadget Cylm drawn in Figure~. We take m disjoint copies of the directed m-cycle DCm arranged in a cylindrical fashion so that there is an edge from i in the jth copy to i in the j+1th copy (drawn in red), and an edge from i in the j+1th copy to i+1 in the jth copy (drawn in green). We consider DCm to have vertices \1,ldots,m\. A key role will be played by Hamilton cycles HC_m in a strongly connected reflexive tournament on m vertices. We consider this cycle also labelled \1,ldots,m\, in order to attach it to the gadget Cylm. The gadget Cylm is an alteration of a gadget that appears in for proving that sc List ensuremathH-Colouring is NP-complete when ensuremathH is an undirected cycle on at least four vertices, but our proof is very different. The following lemma follows from induction on the copies of DCm, since a reflexive tournament has no double edges. In any homomorphism h from Cylm, with bottom cycle DCm, to a reflexive tournament, if |h(DCm)|=1, then |h(Cylm)|=1. We will use another property, denoted (dagger), of Cylm, which is that the retractions from Cylm to its bottom copy of DCm, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of DCm. That is, the top copy of DCm is mapped isomorphically to the bottom copy, and all such isomorphisms may be realised. The reason is that in such a retraction, the (j+1)th copy may either map under the identity to the jth copy, or rotate one edge of the cycle clockwise, and Cylm consists of sufficiently many (namely m) copies of DCm. Now let ensuremathH be a reflexive tournament that contains a subtournament~ensuremathH_0 on m vertices that is endo-trivial. By Lemma~, we find that ensuremathH_0 contains at least one directed Hamilton cycle HC_0. Define Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]) as follows. Begin with ensuremathH and add a copy of the gadget Cylm, where the bottom copy of DCm is identified with HC_0, to build a digraph~ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0). Now ask, for some y in V(ensuremathH) whether there is a retraction r of ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0) to ensuremathH so that some vertex x in the top copy of DCm in Cylm is such that r(x)=y. Such vertices y comprise the set Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]). Remark~1. If x belongs to some copy of DCm that is not the top copy, we can find a vertex~x' in the top copy of DCm and a retraction r' from ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0) to ensuremathH with r'(x')=r(x)=y, namely by letting r' map the vertices of higher copies of~DCm to the image of their corresponding vertex in the copy that contains~x. In particular this implies that Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]) contains V(ensuremathH_0). We now observe that Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0])=V(ensuremathH) if ensuremathH retracts to~ensuremathH_0. setlengthunitlength3947sp begingroupmakeatletterifxSetFigFontundefined This tournament does not retract to the DC^*_3 on the left-hand side, yet Spill_3(ensuremathH[DC^*_3,DC_3]) = V(ensuremathH). We now need to deal with the situation in which we have an isomorphic copy ensuremathH'_0=i(ensuremathH_0) of ensuremathH_0 in ensuremathH with Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH'_0,i(HC_0)])=V(ensuremathH), such that ensuremathH does not retract to ensuremathH'_0 (see Figure~ for an example). We cannot deal with this case in a direct matter and first show another base case. For this we need the following lemma and an extension of endo-triviality that we discuss afterwards. Let ensuremathH be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament ensuremathH_0 so that any endomorphism of ensuremathH that fixes ensuremathH_0 is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism of ensuremathH that maps ensuremathH_0 to an isomorphic copy ensuremathH'_0=i(ensuremathH_0) of itself is an automorphism of ensuremathH. For contradiction, suppose there is an endomorphism h that maps ensuremathH_0 to an isomorphic copy ensuremathH'_0=i(ensuremathH_0) of itself that is not an automorphism of ensuremathH. In particular, |h(ensuremathH)|<|V(ensuremathH)|. Choose h^-1 in the following fashion. We let h^-1 of h(ensuremathH_0) be the natural isomorphism of h(ensuremathH_0) to ensuremathH_0 (that inverts the isomorphism given by h from ensuremathH_0 to ensuremathH'_0). We usually visualise the right-hand copy of DC^*_4 as the ``bottom'' copy and then we talk about vertices ``above'' and ``below'' according to the red arrows. subsectionThe NP-Hardness Gadget We now introduce the gadget Cylm drawn in Figure~. We take m disjoint copies of the directed m-cycle DCm arranged in a cylindrical fashion so that there is an edge from i in the jth copy to i in the j+1th copy (drawn in red), and an edge from i in the j+1th copy to i+1 in the jth copy (drawn in green). We consider DCm to have vertices \1,ldots,m\. A key role will be played by Hamilton cycles HC_m in a strongly connected reflexive tournament on m vertices. We consider this cycle also labelled \1,ldots,m\, in order to attach it to the gadget Cylm. The gadget Cylm is an alteration of a gadget that appears in for proving that sc List ensuremathH-Colouring is NP-complete when ensuremathH is an undirected cycle on at least four vertices, but our proof is very different. The following lemma follows from induction on the copies of DCm, since a reflexive tournament has no double edges. In any homomorphism h from Cylm, with bottom cycle DCm, to a reflexive tournament, if |h(DCm)|=1, then |h(Cylm)|=1. We will use another property, denoted (dagger), of Cylm, which is that the retractions from Cylm to its bottom copy of DCm, once propagated through the intermediate copies, induce on the top copy precisely the set of automorphisms of DCm. That is, the top copy of DCm is mapped isomorphically to the bottom copy, and all such isomorphisms may be realised. The reason is that in such a retraction, the (j+1)th copy may either map under the identity to the jth copy, or rotate one edge of the cycle clockwise, and Cylm consists of sufficiently many (namely m) copies of DCm. Now let ensuremathH be a reflexive tournament that contains a subtournament~ensuremathH_0 on m vertices that is endo-trivial. By Lemma~, we find that ensuremathH_0 contains at least one directed Hamilton cycle HC_0. Define Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]) as follows. Begin with ensuremathH and add a copy of the gadget Cylm, where the bottom copy of DCm is identified with HC_0, to build a digraph~ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0). Now ask, for some y in V(ensuremathH) whether there is a retraction r of ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0) to ensuremathH so that some vertex x in the top copy of DCm in Cylm is such that r(x)=y. Such vertices y comprise the set Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]). Remark~1. If x belongs to some copy of DCm that is not the top copy, we can find a vertex~x' in the top copy of DCm and a retraction r' from ensuremathF(ensuremathH_0,HC_0) to ensuremathH with r'(x')=r(x)=y, namely by letting r' map the vertices of higher copies of~DCm to the image of their corresponding vertex in the copy that contains~x. In particular this implies that Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0]) contains V(ensuremathH_0). We now observe that Spill_m(ensuremathH[ensuremathH_0,HC_0])=V(ensuremathH) if ensuremathH retracts to~ensuremathH_0. setlengthunitlength3947sp begingroupmakeatletterifxSetFigFontundefined Let ensuremathH be a reflexive tournament, containing a subtournament ensuremathH_0 so that any endomorphism of ensuremathH that fixes ensuremathH_0 is an automorphism. Then any endomorphism of ensuremathH that maps ensuremathH_0 to an isomorphic copy ensuremathH'_0=i(ensuremathH_0) of itself is an automorphism of ensuremathH.
